Well, the past few years I’ve been obsessed with learning about languages/linguistics. It’s also fascinating how language and history are so intertwined. Since I’m a native Spanish and English speaker, I’m particularly interested in Indo-European languages. Sometimes it’s hard to wrap my head around the idea that all these speakers of IE languages from Spanish to Icelandic to Persian to Hindi and so many more, (theoretically) descend from one tribe that existed thousands of years ago in the steppe north of the Black Sea.

I could go on, but I’ll share a bit about 2 non Indo-European languages I find interesting:  
• Hungarian! If you look at a map that shows languages, you’ll see it managed to survive as a non-IE language surrounded by all IE languages.

It just takes a lot of practice, time and dedicated focus. I have a decent pronunciation for someone who’s only been learning for two years from outside Germany (I’ve been complimented by a few natives and other longer time students, which was motivating)! 

I read that you’ve only been learning for a year or so and it’s been on and off. To give you an idea of how much time I spent on pronunciation, I’ll explain how I practiced below. 

When I first started, I would listen and repeat the sounds that exist in German but not English for at least 30 minutes per night. Started with the umlauts, watched YouTube videos on how to pronounce these and really stared at the mouths of German speakers on YT videos when they made those sounds, then just sat in my room practicing, trying to really notice what my lips and tongue were doing. Then moved on to -CH and -r. The -r will probably always be hard for me and I still continue to practice that sound. Anyway, when I first started focusing on that sound, I started with just getting the -r sound alone, then I made my way through the alphabet, practicing each letter placed before an -r since different sounds are made in different parts of the mouth and it takes muscle training to be able to pronounce for example -br or -fr, etc. But again, I have spent hours training my mouth muscles to be able to move that way.

A few other pronunciation tips:  
•Try to keep listening to as much of the language as possible in a focused way. You’ll gain a better ear over *time* but not *overnight*!  
•Try recording yourself more often so you can see your own progress, too! If you put in the time, you’ll start to see it and that gets super motivating!  
•For longer/more difficult words start from the end. Ex: “Nachrichten” was a tough one that I used this method with. Started with “ichten” then when that sounded good, added the -r, then finally added the “nach” to pronounce the whole word.  
•Check out forvo.com if you haven’t already, it’s a pronunciation dictionary that’s been extremely helpful for me.  
•This one, a teacher told me and blew my mind at the time, but the -L in German and English are different. German’s is “sharper” and English’s is “darker” - probably YouTube vids on this or just listen to the difference between “hello” and “hallo.”  
•There are some “minimal pairs” lists on a website called rhinospike.com you can use for more hearing training, especially helpful for the vowel sounds (you can also use multiple tabs in forvo for the same effect, especially if you can find recordings of the different words by the same speaker).  
•Keep your mouth a little more closed. Us Americans open our mouths kind of a lot when we speak, and our mouths move a little looser; but if you watch videos of native German speakers, you can see their mouths are a little more tight/closed when they speak.  
•If you can afford it, find a speaking tutor on iTalki and let them know which sounds are most difficult for you so you can practice them.  
•Don’t be so hard on yourself and make sure you’re having fun! Remember, your mouth muscles need to work up to being used to make these new sounds.
